table.title: Distributed Systems Glossary
table.html:
TermDefinitionExample
IdempotencyProperty of an operation that produces the same observable result whether it is executed once or repeated with identical input, allowing safe retries after timeouts.A payment API accepts a client-supplied request key so a retried charge is not posted twice.
Eventual consistencyReplication model in which updates propagate asynchronously and replicas may temporarily disagree, but converge to the same state once writes stop and reconciliation completes.A user changes a profile photo; followers see it within seconds, though two regions may briefly show different versions.
BackpressureFlow-control mechanism by which a downstream consumer signals its capacity limits to an upstream producer, preventing unbounded queues, memory growth, and overload.A log shipper pauses reads when the indexing service reports its buffer above 80 percent.
Circuit breakerResilience pattern that monitors calls to a failing dependency and temporarily rejects requests after a threshold, giving the dependency time to recover instead of amplifying load.After five consecutive checkout timeouts, the client fails fast for 30 seconds before probing the service again.
QuorumMinimum number of replicas that must acknowledge a read or write for the operation to be considered valid, typically a majority in odd-sized clusters to avoid split-brain decisions.In a five-node cluster, a write succeeds after three nodes persist it and a read contacts three nodes.
Write-ahead logDurability technique in which changes are appended to a sequential log and flushed before being applied to the main data structure, enabling recovery after a crash.A database records each transaction in the WAL, then updates its B-tree pages during the next checkpoint.
CAP theoremTheorem stating that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency, availability, and partition tolerance; during a network partition, designers must choose between consistency and availability.A payment ledger favors consistency and rejects writes when it cannot reach a majority of replicas.
table.brief: Glossary: term as row header (some long like "Eventual consistency"), definition (long), example (medium)

understanding.purpose: Define distributed-systems terms and illustrate each with an example.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the first column for a term, then read across its row to connect the definition with the example. Wrapped lines should remain easy to associate with their row.
groups: Definition and Example are companion prose columns: one explains the term and the other makes it concrete.
Term is the row identifier and needs enough prominence to support scanning.
keep_intact: Individual words and technical identifiers, especially long terms and unbreakable words in the prose.
The association between each term, its definition and its example.
may_wrap: Multiword terms can wrap between words.
Definitions and examples can wrap naturally at word boundaries; longer cells can absorb additional lines in the other cells of the same row.

preferred.name: r2B
preferred.note: Move one pixel from Definition to Example relative to r1A. Test a small improvement to example measure while keeping more definition width than r1B or r1C.

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Keep Term at the minimum that preserves Backpressure and give Example the minimum needed for its longest word. Use the remaining pixel to widen Definition relative to r2B; check whether this recovers better definition wrapping while preserving all words.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Move 5px from definition to example while keeping all three columns above their measured unbreakable-word minimums. Test whether examples gain more natural line breaks without making definitions markedly taller.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Give the term column a small buffer beyond its measured minimum and retain most of the definition width. Test whether this improves identifier spacing without substantially increasing row height.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Keep the term column intact and give Example more room to test a more balanced pair of prose columns. Definition remains above its longest-word minimum, though its increased wrapping may make some rows taller.

bad.name: r2A
bad.note: Give Definition one more pixel while retaining the minimum 83px text width needed by Example. Test whether this improves definition wrapping without making examples materially worse.
bad.why: The example column splits “consecutive” across lines, interrupting the sentence for a small gain in definition width.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: Test whether reducing Term by one pixel still keeps its longest labels intact in the browser, using the recovered space for Definition. The stated text-width estimate puts this just below the 99px threshold, so the render must be checked for splitting or overflow.
bad.why: The row label “Backpressure” splits mid-word, weakening the term a reader needs to find and identify.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Give Definition the maximum width available while keeping the term intact, accepting the known split in Example as a comparison point for whether improved definition wrapping materially changes the table’s rhythm.
bad.why: The example column splits “consecutive” across lines, while the unused pixel could prevent the break.

rationale: r2B and r3A keep the row labels and prose words intact while giving the longest column, Definition, the most space. Their rows have the same heights and very similar wrapping, so the one-pixel exchange between Definition and Example does not produce a meaningful visual advantage. The term column remains wide enough for “Backpressure,” and the shaded row headers keep each long entry identifiable.

general: Protect row identifiers and unbreakable words when allocating narrow columns.
Give width according to each column’s reading role and content, while judging the resulting rows as units.
A shorter table is not an improvement if it introduces distracting word breaks.
specific: The term column needs about 120 px to keep “Backpressure” intact.
An example width of 103 px splits “consecutive” in the supplied renders; 104 px avoids that split.

tradeoffs: The wider example column in r1B and r3B gives examples more breathing room, but leaves definitions more fragmented and makes the table taller. A designer might accept the isolated example-word split in r2A for its shorter table.
uncertain: The ranges describe the tested preferred allocations, not a verified continuous interval: changing one column requires adjusting the others to stay within 359 px, and other nearby combinations were not rendered.

critique.good: The term column keeps individual terms intact and makes the row identifiers easy to scan. Headers are clear, and the two prose columns remain associated within each bordered row.
critique.problems: Definitions form tall, narrow blocks, while examples often finish much earlier, leaving substantial empty space within rows. The example column also wraps into many short lines.
critique.cause: The 120px term column is just wide enough for its longest word, leaving 135px for definitions and 104px for examples. Both prose columns are constrained, but the longer definitions drive most row heights.

critique.good: The wider definition column produces more readable phrases and shorter rows. Examples also have a little more room than in r0A.
critique.problems: Several row identifiers visibly break inside words, including Idempotency, consistency and Backpressure. That damages the first column's primary scanning function, despite the reported split count.
critique.cause: At 95px, the term column provides only 74px of text width, less than the 99px needed by its longest unbreakable word. The extra definition width comes at the expense of intact identifiers.

critique.good: The wider example column gives examples more natural phrases and makes them easier to read across from the definitions.
critique.problems: Term identifiers and long definition words visibly split, and definitions become very tall stacks of short lines. Examples frequently end far above the bottom of their rows, weakening the visual balance between the companion columns.
critique.cause: The 110px term column provides 89px of text width, below the 99px needed, and the 120px definition column provides 99px, below its 108px longest word. Giving 129px to examples leaves too little space for the longer definitions.

critique.good: The term column is easy to scan, headers stay on one line, and words remain intact. The wider definition column gives the longer prose a useful advantage; this is the most compact of the three renders.
critique.problems: Definitions still form tall, narrow blocks, especially in CAP theorem. Examples often finish much earlier, leaving large empty areas within already tall rows.
critique.cause: At 135px, Definition has only 114px for text. Example has 83px, enough to keep its longest word intact but too little for comfortable prose; the 120px term column also leaves substantial unused space below short labels.

critique.good: The 109px example column makes some examples less cramped, while the term labels and headers remain clear and words stay intact.
critique.problems: Definitions become more fragmented, with noticeably taller rows for Eventual consistency, Backpressure and CAP theorem. The extra example space does not compensate for the loss of definition width across the table.
critique.cause: Reducing Definition from 135px to 130px leaves 109px for text, barely above its longest unbreakable word. Small changes in line breaks add several lines to long cells.

critique.good: The term column preserves clear row identification, and the prose stays within the viewport without mid-word splits.
critique.problems: The wider term column gives little visible benefit over r1A, while definitions wrap more and several rows grow taller. Examples remain as narrow as in r1A.
critique.cause: Moving 2px from Definition to Term leaves Definition at 133px and Term at 122px; the extra term width does not prevent the multiword labels from wrapping.

critique.good: The bold term column supports scanning, and the wider definition column gives the longer prose priority. Row borders keep each definition and example associated.
critique.problems: The example breaks “consecutive” across lines in the Circuit breaker row. The narrow prose columns also produce tall rows and leave substantial empty space beneath many examples.
critique.cause: The 103px example column leaves only 82px for text, just short of the longest unbreakable word. The 120px term column preserves the longest term but leaves limited width for both prose columns.

critique.good: All words stay intact, headers fit, and the term column remains easy to scan. The example has a little more room, improving its line breaks and making it a better companion to the definition.
critique.problems: Definitions remain very narrow and fragmented; the Quorum row becomes taller than in r2A. Long rows and uneven amounts of white space make cross-row scanning laborious.
critique.cause: Increasing Example to 105px avoids the word split, but reducing Definition to 134px gives it only 113px of text width.

critique.good: The wider definition column improves several line breaks and shortens the first and last data rows. The hierarchy and row boundaries remain clear.
critique.problems: “Backpressure” splits in the term column, damaging the key scanning label; “consecutive” also splits in the example. The shorter table comes at the cost of word integrity.
critique.cause: The 119px term column leaves 98px for a 99px word, and the 103px example column leaves 82px for an 83px word.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r2A.why: The term and definition columns scan reasonably well, but the narrow example column breaks 'consecutive' across lines and makes examples choppy.

r1B.why: Terms remain intact and examples read reasonably well, though the narrow definition column creates many short lines and a lengthy table.

ref_equal.why: The nearly equal columns split 'Backpressure' and long definition words across lines, weakening both row identification and reading flow.

ref_auto.why: Terms and long words remain intact, and the definition has useful space. Examples still wrap into short lines, but rows remain easy to associate.

r2B.why: The definition has room for relatively natural phrases, terms remain intact, and examples avoid the mid-word break visible in A. The narrow columns still make rows tall.

r1C.why: The columns preserve terms and long words while giving the definitions useful space. Examples are narrow but legible, and the row structure remains clear.

raw.unsure: D, E and F are close; their small width differences make the choice sensitive to individual line breaks. All are constrained by the phone width and have tall rows.

ref_equal.why: The near-equal columns leave the definition cramped and split words, including the row label Backpressure. Long rows contain substantial empty space beside the definitions.

r1B.why: Row labels remain intact and the definition has more room, but the narrow example column produces many short lines and an uneven distribution of white space.

r2A.why: The wider definition column improves the densest text and keeps row labels intact, but the example column splits consecutive across lines.

r2B.why: Row labels and words remain intact, while the definition has enough space to read reasonably well. Examples are still narrow and require frequent wrapping.

r1C.why: The columns keep labels and words intact and give the definition more space than the example. Both prose columns remain narrow, making rows tall.

ref_auto.why: The compact labels leave room for the longer definition, and words stay intact. The example column is narrow but remains readable.

raw.unsure: D, E and F are very close; their small differences in wrapping do not produce a clear overall winner. All three involve substantial wrapping at this viewport width.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
